question:
Patient note:
A 72-year-old male presented to the outpatient internal-medicine clinic for evaluation of progressive exertional calf discomfort and subacute epigastric burning that has worsened over the past month. He reports that over the last year he has been able to walk only about two city blocks before cramping pain develops in both lower legs, most prominently on the right; the discomfort predictably resolves within a few minutes of rest and recurs on resumption of ambulation, and he now avoids his usual morning walks because of this limitation. He recalls undergoing a duplex ultrasound at another facility approximately three years ago that demonstrated diminished flow in the superficial femoral artery, and at that time his primary care physician started him on daily aspirin and a high-intensity statin. He has never undergone angioplasty or bypass surgery and denies any prior chest pain, myocardial infarction, or episodes of decompensated heart function. In the same time frame he has also developed intermittent gnawing pain in the upper abdomen, occasionally radiating to the back, most often two to three hours after meals or when he skips breakfast; the discomfort is partially relieved by over-the-counter antacids. About eight years ago he underwent an upper endoscopy that revealed a 1-cm clean-based duodenal lesion that was treated with a short course of proton-pump inhibition; he completed an H. pylori eradication regimen and has had no hematemesis, melena, or need for blood transfusion since then. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed at age 63, currently managed with metformin 1000 mg twice daily; his last documented hemoglobin A1c obtained two months earlier was 7.1%, and he denies visual changes, numbness or tingling in the feet, hypoglycemic episodes, or prior hospitalizations for diabetic ketoacidosis. He has never been told he has kidney problems, his most recent serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL, and urinalysis did not reveal proteinuria. He does not smoke cigarettes and consumes alcohol only on social occasions. He denies chronic cough, wheezing, or dyspnea at rest, and has never used inhalers or supplemental oxygen. There is no history of transient neurologic deficits, cerebrovascular accidents, seizures, memory impairment, or gradual cognitive decline; his family confirms that he manages his own finances and independently performs all activities of daily living. He has no prior liver disease, viral hepatitis, jaundice, ascites, or encephalopathy, and his bilirubin, ALT, AST, and INR checked during last year’s annual physical were within reference limits. He has never been diagnosed with connective tissue disorders, systemic vasculitides, HIV infection, hematologic malignancies, or solid-organ cancers and has not undergone chemotherapy or radiation therapy. Surgical history is notable only for an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy performed at age 58 for symptomatic gallstones. Current medications include metformin as noted, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 81 mg daily, and occasional omeprazole 20 mg as needed; he takes no anticoagulants, corticosteroids, or NSAIDs. On review of systems he endorses the lower-extremity exertional pain and postprandial epigastric discomfort but denies weight loss, night sweats, fevers, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, edema, claudication of the upper extremities, hematuria, or tarry stools. Vital signs in clinic show blood pressure 136/74 mmHg bilaterally, heart rate 78 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97% on ambient air, and temperature 36.8 °C. He is alert, oriented, and conversant, in no acute distress. Cardiovascular examination reveals normal S1 and S2 with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops; jugular venous pressure is not elevated. Peripheral pulses are palpable but diminished (1+) at bilateral dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries, with normal femoral pulses and no bruits; there is no lower-extremity edema. Pulmonary auscultation demonstrates clear breath sounds without wheezes or crackles. Abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness to deep palpation, no guarding or rebound, liver span percussed at 9 cm in the mid-clavicular line, and no splenomegaly or ascites. Neurologic examination shows intact cranial nerves, full strength and sensation in all extremities, symmetrical reflexes, and normal gait aside from voluntary limitation because of calf pain. Skin is warm without ulcers or cyanosis, though there is loss of hair over the anterior shins. Laboratory studies drawn today include complete blood count with hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.2 × 10⁹/L, platelets 220 × 10⁹/L, basic metabolic panel notable for fasting glucose 142 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73 m², BUN 14 mg/dL, electrolytes within normal limits, AST 22 U/L, ALT 18 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 72 U/L, and total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL; lipase is 24 U/L. An ankle-brachial index will be arranged to better quantify lower-extremity perfusion, and the patient is scheduled for repeat esophagogastroduodenoscopy to assess the status of his prior ulcer given the recurrence of dyspeptic symptoms.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) adds age points to weighted comorbidity points:
- Age 72: the 70–79 age band contributes 3 points.
- Peripheral vascular disease: exertional calf pain relieved by rest, diminished pedal pulses, and prior duplex evidence of reduced femoral arterial flow support intermittent claudication → 1.
- Peptic ulcer disease: prior endoscopically documented duodenal ulcer → 1; active bleeding is not required.
- Diabetes without documented end-organ damage: treated type 2 diabetes with no reported diabetic renal, neurologic, or retinal complications → 1.
- No other qualifying CCI conditions are documented → 0.
Sum: 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 6.
Final answer: 6
